tldr: Focusing on what event cameras fundamentally measure—moving contrast edges—this study builds an ultra-fast simulator that bypasses costly visual rendering to synthesize events directly from scene geometry. An obstacle avoidance policy is trained via reinforcement learning in just 34 minutes, achieving fully autonomous flight (82% average success rate) on a low-power microcontroller onboard a 56 g nano-drone.

overview:
Event cameras are bio-inspired sensors whose pixels asynchronously detect brightness changes with microsecond temporal resolution. Featuring extremely low latency, high dynamic range (>120 dB), and milliwatt-level power consumption, they are ideal sensors for agile nano-drones. However, applying reinforcement learning (RL) to autonomous flight with these sensors hits a massive bottleneck in simulation. Conventional simulators render high-frame-rate synthetic images first before computing per-pixel intensity changes, making the large number of training steps prohibitively slow.

The authors tackled this with a bold simplification: "Isn't an event camera fundamentally just detecting the moment geometric edges move?" Instead of rendering photorealistic images, they built an "analytic event proxy" that synthesizes event frames directly from 3D obstacle contour edge points and drone ego-motion via geometric equations. This achieved an astonishing generation speed of just $17\,\mu\text{s}$ per frame—over $400\times$ faster than conventional rendering pipelines.

Using this proxy to train goal-directed obstacle avoidance end-to-end, RL training converged in just 34 minutes. Furthermore, without any fine-tuning or additional learning, the trained policy zero-shot transferred to a ray-traced photorealistic physical simulator (Isaac Sim) and real hardware with a Prophesee GenX320 sensor. In real-flight experiments using a 56 g Crazyflie drone and an STM32N6 microcontroller board running a 1.2 MB int8 model, the drone achieved an average navigation success rate of 82% across three obstacle courses without relying on external PCs or motion capture.
contributions: Developed an analytic simulator that completely eliminates visual rendering to synthesize events directly from scene geometry and ego-motion, slashing RL training time from days down to about 30 minutes (a 3-order-of-magnitude speedup).
Demonstrated that a policy trained purely in a simple proxy environment zero-shot transfers directly to ray-traced physics-based Isaac Sim and real-world hardware sensors.

Achieved the first fully onboard goal-directed navigation on a 56 g nano-drone equipped with an event camera and a commercial low-power microcontroller, running perception and inference entirely on the aircraft.

sections.heading: The Weight and Simulation Barriers Blocking Nano-Drone Autonomy
sections.summary: Nano-drones navigating tight spaces face severe weight and power constraints, ruling out heavy depth cameras and GPUs. Event cameras are promising, but simulation speed required for reinforcement learning has been a fatal bottleneck. This paper solves the problem with an analytic simulator that discards visual rendering.
sections.details:
Nano-drones hold great promise for navigating cluttered, GPS-denied environments, but autonomous navigation remains extremely challenging. Conventional SLAM pipelines and depth cameras (such as the Intel RealSense D435i, weighing ~72 g and consuming 3.5 W) are far too heavy and power-hungry for platforms weighing only tens of grams, rapidly draining their batteries. Time-of-Flight (ToF) arrays are lightweight, but their resolution is too coarse (e.g., $8{\times}8$ zones) to detect thin poles or wires. In addition, these platforms cannot carry embedded GPUs like the NVIDIA Jetson, which weigh 70–100 g and draw 10–25 W.

Event cameras offer an appealing alternative. Because only pixels undergoing intensity changes trigger events with microsecond precision, they consume milliwatt-level power and remain completely free from motion blur even during aggressive rotations. However, when attempting to train end-to-end control policies via reinforcement learning, the sluggishness of simulators becomes a major roadblock. Existing event simulators render computer graphics images at high frame rates before taking intensity differences, making the tens of millions of interaction steps required for RL unbearably slow.

Observing that event cameras fundamentally capture "moving contrast edges," this study proposes an "analytic event proxy" that completely bypasses visual rendering. Generating a frame in an ultra-fast $17\,\mu\text{s}$, the system completes policy training in just 34 minutes and realizes fully onboard autonomous flight on a 56 g Crazyflie.

sections.heading: How Did Prior Works Tackle This, and Where Did They Fall Short?
sections.summary: While event-based drone flight and fast simulation have been explored before, past works relied on GPU-equipped platforms or offline imitation learning. This study bridges end-to-end reinforcement learning and real flight on an ultra-low-power microcontroller for the first time.
sections.details:
### II-A Event-Based Drone Flight
Existing event-based flight approaches fall into indirect methods—which first estimate optical flow, time-to-contact, or depth before computing control inputs—and direct methods that output control actions straight from raw events. While both have shown impressive results, they either offload processing to a ground-station PC or rely on larger drones carrying power-hungry (10 W+) NVIDIA Jetson boards. On the other end of the spectrum, extreme low-power flight has been explored with neuromorphic processors like Intel Loihi, but goal-directed navigation through cluttered environments using affordable off-the-shelf microcontrollers remained uncharted territory.

### II-B Simulating Event Cameras
Interactive simulation environments are vital for reinforcement learning, but conventional event simulators (such as ESIM and EVIS) follow a pipeline of first rendering high-resolution, high-frame-rate images and then converting them into events. Recent work (Messikommer et al.) avoided online rendering by turning to imitation learning from privileged information, yet still depended on pre-rendered offline datasets. This paper completely dispenses with pre-rendered datasets, directly generating event frames from analytical formulas inside the simulation loop.

### II-C Nano-Drones and Learning-Based Flight Control
Autonomous flight under gram-level and milliwatt-level constraints has historically been achieved using carefully hand-crafted lightweight algorithms or small frame-based neural networks (such as the PULP series). However, this work is the first to integrate all three elements: end-to-end reinforcement learning, event-based vision, and onboard inference on a nano-scale microcontroller.

sections.heading: Trading Rendering for Analytical Edges: Fast Simulation and Microcontroller Deployment
sections.summary: The authors model event frame generation directly from image-plane line sweeps of geometric edge points induced by ego-motion. The framework provides an end-to-end pipeline: RL via PPO, validation in Isaac Sim, and int8 quantized deployment on an STM32N6 microcontroller.
sections.details:
### III-A Event Proxy Generative Model
Matching the operating mode of the target sensor (Prophesee GenX320), the proxy directly outputs signed event-count frames ($64{\times}64$ pixels) accumulated over a 20 ms exposure window. The environment is represented not as polygon meshes, but as 3D edge point clouds capturing obstacle silhouettes and wall boundaries. Using the camera's linear velocity $\mathbf{v}$ and angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}$, the sweep trajectory of each edge point on the image plane is computed via pinhole projection, and event mass is accumulated along this line segment. Event counts are modeled using a saturating ramp function derived from the geometric sweeping of subpixel patches, while polarities (ON/OFF) are determined physically from edge normal vectors and the motion direction (whether an edge occludes or reveals the background). Ground plane textures and occlusions (via a coarse z-buffer) are also handled analytically. Five simulation parameters were calibrated once against statistical metrics (such as event firing rates and median counts) gathered from 10 seconds of hand-held sensor data in an office.

### III-B Reinforcement Learning Setup
The task is to navigate toward a goal without collisions in a $22{\times}22\,\text{m}$ room cluttered with obstacles. The policy input consists of a temporal stack of the 3 most recent event frames, combined with a 4-dimensional context vector containing linear speed, angular velocity, and relative heading to the goal. The policy outputs 2 degrees of freedom: yaw rate and forward velocity. The control loop is fixed at 13.3 Hz to match the microcontroller inference budget. The reward function combines goal progress with a potential-based shaping term based on distance to obstacle surfaces. Training uses standard PPO with a compact convolutional network of only 1.12M parameters.

### III-C Sim-to-Sim Verification (Isaac Sim)
Before deploying on hardware, the trained policy is evaluated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim equipped with a ray-tracing renderer and the EVIS plugin. Events are photorealistically generated at a native $320{\times}320$ resolution and downsampled to $64{\times}64$ following the real hardware firmware pipeline. This tests zero-shot generalization in an environment packed with heavy textures and cast shadows absent from the training proxy.

### III-D Microcontroller Implementation
The trained model was quantized to int8 via ONNX and compiled for the Neural-ART NPU on an STM32N6 microcontroller, producing a binary of just 1.2 MB. The system runs an asynchronous architecture: the Crazyflie flight controller (STM32F405) communicates with the N6 board over UART, streaming optical-flow-derived odometry (goal heading and velocity) to the N6, while the Crazyflie tracks the N6's inferred velocity setpoints via an internal 500 Hz control loop.

captions.F2: Generative pipeline of the rendering-free event proxy. (a) The environment is represented as 3D edge point clouds, (b) projected and swept across the image plane by camera ego-motion. (c) Event generation is governed by a saturation function of pixel-patch sweep area, and (d) signed accumulation rapidly synthesizes event frames that closely mimic real sensor output.

sections.heading: Real-World Deployment After 34 Minutes of Training: Sim Comparisons and 56 g Drone Flight
sections.summary: The proposed proxy reaches a speed of 17 microseconds per frame, finishing RL training in 34 minutes on a single RTX 4090. The policy achieved an 83% success rate in unseen Isaac Sim environments and 82% in real-world drone flights, proving practical environmental robustness.
sections.details:
### IV-A Evaluation Setup and Metrics
A 30-episode evaluation protocol was established in Isaac Sim across randomized obstacle layouts under two conditions: a "shadow" environment dominated by geometry and lighting shadows, and a "texture" environment with dense patterns across floors and walls. Metrics include AvoidBench standards such as success rate (SR), average goal velocity (AGV), and path optimality (PO).

### IV-B Zero-Shot Transfer and Simulation Performance
The policy zero-shot transferred from the proxy training environment to unseen Isaac Sim scenes without any fine-tuning, reaching an 83% success rate (AGV 2.38 m/s) in the shadow environment and retaining 70% (AGV 1.62 m/s) in the texture environment. The slight performance dip in the textured scene stems from background surface patterns absent from the proxy, which doubled the event density, yet the policy showed remarkable resilience. The int8 quantized model maintained virtually identical performance to the fp32 baseline.

### IV-C Comparison with Baselines
The method was benchmarked against several baselines: (1) A privileged PPO policy trained on ground-truth depth images (an upper bound) scored 100%/97%, while this monocular event-based approach stayed competitive at 83%/70%. (2) An insect-inspired reactive optical flow balancing rule failed drastically, achieving only 13–17% success. (3) PPO trained directly inside the Isaac Sim rendering loop for a full 24 hours only managed 195k steps due to slow rendering, stalling at a 40–53% success rate. The proposed proxy synthesizes frames in $17\,\mu\text{s}$, more than $400\times$ faster than the rendering pipeline (6.9 ms). Reaching the same 40 million steps would take an estimated 200 GPU-days with rendering, whereas the proxy completes training in just 34 minutes.

### IV-D Real-Flight Experiments
Equipped with a GenX320 sensor and the N6 board, the 56 g Crazyflie was tested in a laboratory arena filled with obstacles (poles, cardboard towers, plants, and partition screens). The policy achieved 5/5 (100%) in Course 1 (poles and boxes), 5/6 (83%) in Course 2 (adding towers and plants), and 4/6 (67%) in Course 3 (densely packed clutter), yielding an overall average success rate of 82%. Crashes only occurred in narrow, highly congested pockets, mirroring the failure modes observed in simulation.

Bottom: complete trajectory plots across 30 evaluation episodes per condition. Blue paths denote successful goal arrivals, and red paths (cross markers) indicate collisions, showing robust traversability despite heavy visual texturing.

Without external motion capture or ground-station compute, the drone smoothly avoids complex obstacles using onboard sensing and microcontroller inference alone.

sections.heading: Discarding Photometry for the Essentials: A New Blueprint for Agile Robotics
sections.summary: By eliminating visual rendering, this analytic simulator breaks the reinforcement learning bottleneck for event cameras. Matching proxy outputs to core sensor statistics opens up a fresh path forward for compute-constrained nano-robotics.
sections.details:
This study introduces a rendering-free methodology for event-based robot navigation. By synthesizing events directly from scene geometry and ego-motion via an analytic simulator, practical navigation policies can be trained in just 34 minutes on a single GPU. The resulting network zero-shot transfers to both physics-based simulators and real-world drones, realizing fully autonomous flight on a featherweight 56 g hardware platform.

The key takeaway is that for sensors whose simulation bottleneck lies in image rendering (photometry), a geometrically principled analytic model matched to output statistics can serve as an effective substitute. While this work focused on planar obstacle avoidance at a fixed altitude, future directions include full 3D acrobatic flight, faster control loops, and dynamic obstacle avoidance.

takeaways: Because event cameras fundamentally measure moving edges, modeling them via pure geometry without CG rendering is sufficient to train reinforcement learning policies that transfer to real hardware.
Slashing simulation step time down to $17\,\mu\text{s}$ allows closed-loop RL that previously took days or weeks to converge in roughly 30 minutes.
Combining a 1.2 MB int8 quantized policy with an event camera enables fully onboard autonomous navigation with zero external dependencies, even on a 56 g drone drawing around 1 W of compute power.
limitations: Because the analytic proxy only models structural edges, dense visual textures on real-world walls and floors cause event densities to surge, leading to a performance drop (from 83% down to 70%).
The current formulation is restricted to 2D planar velocity control at a fixed altitude; aggressive 3D maneuvers involving roll and pitch, as well as dynamic obstacles, remain open challenges.
Microcontroller inference and frame-assembly overhead cap the control frequency at 13.3 Hz, leaving the microsecond-level low-latency potential of event cameras partially untapped.
